The founder's numbers are pinned to the launch era (the founder's gap-11 rule): the YC company page as captured on

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about my work, it makes sense to check straight away whether I work at the kind of place the study is about.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job, and I understand the question on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know without thinking that I work in a hotel group's central reservations office in Munich.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover every case for a plain factual screener, and no escape is needed here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of German hotel groups with a central office or call center, and shows me nothing of a product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question of 18 words with a simple yes-or-no that I can answer after hearing it once.

screens.why1: Right after asking where I work, it makes sense to check whether I actually took booking calls recently before asking about one.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are the words I use every day, so I understand it at first reading.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether booking calls came in on my shifts this week, though on a trade-fair week the answer is obviously yes.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but two escape chips is one too many for a gate, and I can't recall one particular shift is odd because the question does not ask me to recall a particular shift.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's booking calls on every shift and shows me nothing of a product or plan, and it does not lean on the unanswered calls.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question followed by yes or no, and I can answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift? Yes / No (no escape chips on this gate).

screens.why1: It follows on from the yes I just gave, but in my office calls come in on every shift, so this only counts how many days I worked.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand the question the first time I hear it.
screens.why3: I know exactly which days I worked last week, including the trade-fair Saturday, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: The numbers 1 to 7 are distinct and complete after my yes on the last screen, and I can't recall fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It keeps to booking calls on my shift, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question and the numbers are easy to hear, but seven options is over the limit of five, even if a run of numbers is easy to hold.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a booking call go unanswered on your shift? 0; 1 to 2; 3 to 4; 5 to 6; or all 7. Or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: After asking how often booking calls came in, it makes sense to ask which part of my week I would most like made easier.
screens.why2: Check-in, check-out rush, booking calls, group requests and rates on every channel are all words I use every day, though in a central office I would say 'my shifts' rather than 'at the desk'.
screens.why3: I can pick calls, emails, group requests or rates from my own week, but I work in a central office in Munich, so the desk and check-in options and the 'shifts at the desk' anchor describe a front-desk colleague's job rather than mine.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and 'None of these' fits, but two of the five are front-desk work I never do, and nothing covers what weighs on me at peak, such as long hold queues or calls stacking up during a trade fair.
screens.why5: It stays with unanswered booking calls as one option among real daily chores, and I can't see any product or founder's language leaking through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five options I can hold, but 'Getting through the check-in and check-out rush' and 'Answering booking emails and group requests' are a mouthful when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of shifts. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Getting through the calls at peak times; Booking calls that ring out unanswered; Answering booking emails; Handling group requests; or Keeping rates right on every channel. Or say None of these.

screens.why1: After being asked how often calls come in and what I would like made easier, it makes sense to ask how the calls nobody picked up went on my last shift.
screens.why2: I understand it, but 'catching the calls nobody picked up' is not how we talk at the desk; I would say missed calls or calls that rang out, and 'how did it go' needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know what I answered and roughly what the queue did, but on a trade-fair Saturday in a central office I would partly guess how many calls others on the shift missed and whether they were called back.
screens.why4: The ladder is in my words and the escape fits, but 'a few', 'some' and 'many' overlap, and the options mix how many rang out with how fast they were called back, so 'many rang out, most called back that day' has no home.
screens.why5: It stays with the founder's unanswered booking calls, and no product or founder's term for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question and five options are allowed, but the options are long clauses with similar openings, so they are hard to hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. How many missed calls got called back? All within minutes; all that same day; some, when there was time; few or none; or there were no missed calls. Or say Someone else did it that shift.
